My teaching is guided by two principles: build foundations students can carry beyond the classroom and design learning appropriate to students’ stage of development.
For early-stage students, I emphasize structured opportunities to build foundational skills and work through unfamiliar problems. For more advanced students, I provide greater room for interpretation, judgment, and the defense of evidence-based decisions while maintaining clear expectations and milestones.
My professional experience in events, hospitality, and business informs the problems students encounter in class, while my research training helps students move from information toward analysis, interpretation, and defensible decision-making.





School of Sport, Tourism and Hospitality Management · Temple University · Spring 2026

Instructor of Record · Writing-Intensive Course · Student Evaluation: 4.35 / 5
I used cases, discussion, and a semester marketing proposal to ask students to evaluate problems from multiple customer, organizational, and stakeholder perspectives. Students were expected not only to make recommendations, but also to justify why those recommendations were defensible.




School of Sport, Tourism and Hospitality Management · Temple University · Fall 2025

Instructor of Record · Student Evaluation: 4.55 / 5
I organized the course around how data are used in practice: cleaning and organizing information, analyzing it, interpreting results, and communicating findings. Excel functions therefore became tools for accomplishing larger analytical tasks rather than isolated commands to memorize.

Gyusang (Kevin) Hwang

Tourism & Hospitality Management


Temple University


 Philadelphia, PA


  Curriculum Vitae 
  Google Scholar 
  ORCID

I am a Ph.D. Candidate in Business Administration with a concentration in Tourism and Sport at Temple University’s Fox School of Business. My research examines how interactions within tourism and hospitality systems shape people, organizations, and places, with planned events as a central setting and complementary work on digital platforms and service relationships.
I use large-scale behavioral data, econometrics, spatial analysis, experiments, and evidence synthesis to examine consequences for businesses, communities, customers, and workers. Before entering academia, I worked across business travel and MICE, mega-events, and hospitality operations. These experiences continue to shape both the questions I study and the applied perspectives I bring into the classroom.
In my teaching, I focus on helping students build foundations they can carry beyond a single course while developing increasingly independent judgment as they advance through the curriculum.

2026–2027 Academic Job Market
I am currently seeking faculty opportunities in tourism, hospitality, events, and related business disciplines.

My research examines how interactions within tourism and hospitality systems shape people, organizations, and places. Planned events provide my most developed empirical setting, with complementary work examining digital platforms, service relationships, consumer behavior, and employee outcomes.
I use large-scale behavioral data, econometrics, spatial analysis, experiments, and evidence synthesis to investigate how these interactions generate economic, social, spatial, organizational, and behavioral consequences.
